issues.legal_issue: A promise to pay customary rent for land delivered into the vendee’s possession during a delayed sale transaction was a reciprocal and essential term of the agreement.
material_facts: The vendor agreed to sell land and delivered possession to the vendee when the agreement was made.
The agreement required the vendee to pay customary rent if the pending litigation delayed execution of the sale deed beyond one year.
The litigation continued for more than one year.
issues.conclusion: The rent promise was reciprocal and an essential part of the agreement to sell.
issues.legal_principle: Whether promises are reciprocal depends on the particular facts. Section 51 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 addresses reciprocal promises to be simultaneously performed. The court also considered the agreement’s true construction under Explanation (ii) to Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.land_sale_agreement: A vendor and a vendee entered into an agreement for the sale of land.
predicates.possession_given_under_rent_arrangement: The vendor gave the vendee possession on an understanding that customary rent would be paid if the sale was delayed beyond a specified period.
predicates.delay_exceeded_one_year: The event specified in the agreement was delayed beyond one year.

issues.definition: When a land-sale agreement gives the vendee possession subject to a rent obligation if completion is delayed beyond the agreed period, and that delay occurs, the rent promise is reciprocal and essential.

issues.legal_issue: A vendee who fails to perform an essential contractual term and is not ready and willing to perform it may be denied specific performance, particularly where the vendee’s conduct makes enforcement inequitable.
material_facts: The vendee took possession of the agricultural land under an obligation to pay customary rent after the delay exceeded one year.
The vendee paid no rent for approximately thirteen years before filing suit and denied liability to pay rent in his replication.
The vendee cultivated and benefited from the land, while the vendor received less than eighteen percent of its market value.
The vendee sought specific performance of the sale agreement.
issues.conclusion: The vendee was not entitled to specific performance because he failed to perform an essential term, failed to prove readiness and willingness to perform it, and his conduct made the discretionary relief inequitable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, including Explanation (ii), requires a plaintiff seeking specific performance to prove performance of, or readiness and willingness to perform, the essential terms according to the contract’s true construction. Section 20, as applicable to the suit, makes specific performance discretionary and permits refusal where enforcement would be inequitable; Explanation (2) addresses when hardship is assessed. Section 51 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 was also considered in relation to reciprocal promises. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and rent_term_unperformed and no_readiness_or_willingness and prolonged_unpaid_occupation and inequitable_hardship

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A party brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.rent_term_unperformed: The plaintiff did not pay rent required by an essential term of the contract.
predicates.no_readiness_or_willingness: The plaintiff failed to prove performance of, or readiness and willingness to perform, the essential term.
predicates.prolonged_unpaid_occupation: The plaintiff retained and used the property for a prolonged period without paying the agreed rent.
predicates.inequitable_hardship: The plaintiff’s nonperformance and use of the property caused hardship to the other party and made enforcement inequitable.

issues.definition: In a suit for specific performance, when the plaintiff leaves an essential rent term unperformed, fails to show readiness and willingness to perform it, and prolonged unpaid use makes enforcement inequitable, specific performance is denied.

issues.legal_issue: A party seeking alternative monetary relief may be denied that relief after prolonged enjoyment of property without paying the rent due for its use.
material_facts: The vendee’s suit sought alternative monetary relief as well as specific performance.
The vendee and his successors enjoyed the land for approximately fifty-five years without paying rent.
issues.conclusion: The respondents were not entitled to the alternative monetary relief.
issues.legal_principle: The court denied the alternative relief because the respondents had enjoyed the land for a prolonged period without paying rent. The judgment cited no statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this ruling.

predicates.alternative_refund_claim: A plaintiff seeking enforcement of a contract also claimed alternative repayment or other monetary relief.
predicates.prolonged_property_enjoyment_without_ren: The plaintiff or those claiming through the plaintiff enjoyed the property for a prolonged period without paying rent.

issues.definition: When an alternative monetary claim accompanies a contract-enforcement claim and the claimant has enjoyed the property for a prolonged period without paying rent, the alternative refund relief is denied.
